articles.title: Nepal foots Rs 10 lakh rescue bill for 6 Indians trekking illegally despite warnings
articles.summary: Nepal spent an estimated Rs 10 lakh (INR) from its disaster management fund to rescue six Indian trekkers who had allegedly entered the restricted Upper
articles.body: Nepal spent an estimated Rs 10 lakh (INR) from its disaster management fund to rescue six Indian trekkers who had allegedly entered the restricted Upper Dolpa region without mandatory permits, ignored warnings against travelling during heavy snowfall and pressed ahead, leaving their guide behind.The group, comprising five trekkers from West Bengal and one from Andhra Pradesh, spent two nights stranded in the mountains before a helicopter evacuated them on Monday. Authorities subsequently charged them NPR 1.6 lakh (approximately Rs 98,000) in permit fees and penalties but reduced the fines considering their physical condition after the ordeal.The six trekkers — Moumita Halder, Piyali Koley, Jajla Trivedi Kumar, Aditya Singha, Diplina Biswas and Rajesh De — were rescued at dawn on Monday from Danigad, around 300km northwest of Kathmandu. The helicopter made three round trips, evacuating two trekkers on each round. All six were taken to Dunai, the Dolpa district headquarters, where they underwent medical examinations and were subsequently discharged. The operation required a civilian helicopter after a Nepal Army aircraft scheduled to arrive on Sunday developed a technical problem and could not fly.Dolpa chief district officer Junu Hamal told TOI that authorities could have imposed a maximum fine of NPR 50,000 (Rs 31,250) on each trekker but instead charged NPR 20,000 (Rs 12,500) per person. The trekkers also paid $40 (Rs 3,800) each towards mandatory permits. "Seeing their condition, we gave them a concession," Hamal said. However, she criticised the group for ignoring repeated warnings from security personnel, local residents and their guide, putting both themselves and rescuers at risk."Such irresponsible behaviour is unacceptable," she said. "Nepal is already struggling to find funds for reconstruction after the devastating flash floods on Aug 26. At a time when we are trying to rebuild affected communities, having to spend precious disaster funds on a rescue necessitated by such carelessness and irresponsible behaviour is extremely frustrating," she said.The district administration had restricted travel to Upper Dolpa from Oct 29 because of heavy snowfall, but the trekkers allegedly left their guide behind and continued towards Shey-Phoksundo lake despite warnings. They became stranded near the Numa La and Baga La mountain passes, and their guide alerted authorities on Saturday evening. Snow and poor mobile connectivity complicated rescue efforts. articles.title: Dutch police offer record €2m reward in hunt for drug lord Jos Leijdekkers
articles.summary: Jos Leijdekkers has been found guilty in absentia of cocaine smuggling and is believed to be in Sierra Leone.
articles.body:
Dutch authorities have offered a record award of €2m (£1.7m/$2.24m) for information leading to the arrest of Jos Leijdekkers, one of Europe's most-wanted men.

The 35-year-old, who is also known as Bolle Jos (Chubby Jos), was previously accused of being "one of the key players in international cocaine trafficking" by Dutch police.

Commenting on the decision to increase the reward ten-fold, Dutch justice minister David van Weel said it was "necessary given the threat that Leijdekkers poses to national security, our democratic rule of law, and the international legal order".

Dutch prosecutors said capturing Leijdekkers was their "highest priority" and any information shared would be kept secret.

He is listed by Europol, the EU's law enforcement agency, as among their most-wanted fugitives.

In January 2025, Dutch police said he was believed to be living in Sierra Leone and going by the name Omar Sherrif.

Images apparently showing Leijdekkers in the company of President Julius Maada Bio and other officials have previously emerged.

Dutch prosecutors have demanded his extradition but Sierra Leone has refused to cooperate, prompting the EU to cut some aid to the country.

West Africa is a major transit point for cocaine trafficking from Latin America.

In 2024, a court in Rotterdam sentenced Leijdekkers in absentia to 24 years in prison after finding him guilty of smuggling ⁠more than seven metric tons of cocaine.

Several other police investigations in the Netherlands are ongoing.

Leijdekkers has also been sentenced to 79 years in prison in Belgium.

Dutch authorities estimate he has made tens of millions of euros from ⁠cocaine smuggling, and accuse him of money laundering and involvement in the use of extreme violence.

articles.title: ICE officer surrenders after grand jury indicts him for running over immigrant with vehicle in Texas
articles.summary: An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer indicted for allegedly running over an immigrant with his vehicle during an enforcement operation in
articles.body: An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer indicted for allegedly running over an immigrant with his vehicle during an enforcement operation in Houston, Texas, surrendered to authorities on Monday.Mario Alberto Morales appeared before the Harris County 488th District Court after a grand jury indicted him on a second-degree aggravated assault charge involving a deadly weapon. He is accused of striking Miguel Parra-Hernandez with his vehicle on October 10, leaving him with a broken leg and ankle.Morales appeared in court wearing a grey suit and purple tie, accompanied by his lawyers David Lindenmuth and former Harris County district attorney Kim Ogg.During the hearing, prosecutors sought a $75,000 bond, citing the "violent nature" of the incident and alleged admissions of prior drug use uncovered during their investigation. Morales' defence team requested a $25,000 bond, arguing that he posed no flight risk or continuing threat to the community.Judge Matthew Peneguy set his bond at $30,000.What happened during the Houston incident?The incident took place on October 10 when Morales was pursuing Parra-Hernandez and another man who had fled during an enforcement operation.ICE had claimed that Parra-Hernandez ran in front of Morales' vehicle as agents attempted to arrest another individual. However, surveillance footage and body-camera recordings released by the Harris County District Attorney's Office have raised questions about the agency's account.The surveillance footage reportedly shows Morales driving his Jeep Cherokee over a median and towards Parra-Hernandez as he ran away. The vehicle appears to strike him from behind before coming to a stop several feet ahead. Parra-Hernandez was subsequently seen on the ground.Morales' body-camera footage also captured him saying, "He got hit with a car, bro," and, "I was coming in and I hit him with the car."Parra-Hernandez was later taken into custody with a broken leg.Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said the footage contradicted ICE's account that the man had stepped in front of the officer's vehicle.Teare said he hoped the indictment would send a message to federal officers that they could be held accountable for their actions."No badge, title, or position places anyone beyond scrutiny or accountability," Harris County Sheriff Ed Gonzalez said after the indictment was announced.ICE calls indictment 'political stunt'Morales' lawyer Lindenmuth has maintained that his client did not deliberately strike Parra-Hernandez, describing the incident as an accident and accusing the district attorney of pursuing a politically motivated prosecution."This officer was doing his job, and a fleeing individual caused the chaotic circumstances that led to this unfortunate incident," Lindenmuth said.ICE also rejected the allegations, describing them as "reckless and false" and calling the indictment a "political stunt".The agency further questioned the authority of local officials to investigate federal officers carrying out their official duties.Morales joined ICE as a federal immigration officer in August 2025 after working in several law enforcement-related roles, including as a corrections officer and a detention and processing officer at the Port Isabel Detention Center.According to his lawyer, he previously served in the Army as a military police officer and paratrooper before being honourably discharged in 2014.If convicted, Morales faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.You use AI every day. articles.title: Man who drugged and raped wife with strangers 'led double life'
articles.summary: Nine men are on trial accused of helping a Stockport man fulfil "barbaric fantasies" against his wife.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains distressing content

A woman who believed she had not had sex for nine years had in fact been regularly drugged and raped by her own husband and a group of strangers "whose depravity knew no bounds", a jury has been told.

Her husband led a "double life", prosecutors said, regularly giving his wife a "stupefying cocktail" of drugs to make her "completely unaware" of the abuse.

He and four men have already pleaded guilty to a series of offences, but the trial of nine other defendants who deny all charges has begun at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court.

Opening the case for the prosecution, Louise Oakley KC said the wife had been "happy" but "the life she knew ended when the police knocked on the front door".

Before the case was opened, trial judge Maurice Greene warned jurors they would be expected to view evidence that could provoke feelings of "upset and anger".

As Oakley opened the case, they were shown videos of the woman, in her sixties, being raped and sexually assaulted while, the prosecution said, she was unconscious.

The jury heard the husband and vicitim had the appearance of a couple looking forward to retirement, who "led busy lives, enjoying their home and garden, socialising with family and friends, holidays abroad – all very much together".

But Oakley said the husband, who is also in his 60s and cannot be named to protect his wife's legal right to anonymity, had since 2004 been sharing videos and images online of himself raping and assaulting his unconscious wife at their family home in the Stockport area of Greater Manchester.

"You may think it difficult to conceive how such offending could get worse, but it did," she told the court.

The jury heard the husband had "talked about" inviting men to their home to rape his wife for years, but began actually doing so from at least 2023.

The men were, the prosecution said, "well aware that she was not conscious, that is why they were there, to use her body whilst she was unaware".

Oakley said when the husband's Samsung Galaxy mobile phone had been seized by police, it acted "like a confession booth" containing his "darkest secrets" and his "barbaric sexual fantasies".

Detectives found more than a million photographs and videos "cataloging" the husband's abuse on that device.

Oakley said the files had provided the police with "almost a script" of both the husband's offending and that of the nine men on trial.

"Their depravity seems to have had no bounds," she said.

"They too were leading double lives. Either creeping in and out of [the home address], in the hours of darkness, quietly and carefully so that they were not seen or heard, or hiding behind the screens of their mobile telephones or computers - no doubt believing they were safe."

The jury heard the men on trial included alleged "contact offenders" including paramedic Jonathan Kirk, 43; taxi driver Philip Wild, 59; amateur football coach Alan Keelan, 42; recruitment agency worker Mohammed Sabir, 28; Jordan Wallace, 31, who worked for a building supplies agency; sheet metal worker Richard Townsend, 37, and Robert Stewart, 70, who was retired.

Two of the men, Daniel Rayner and David Graves, were described as alleged "non-contact" offenders, who did not attend the victim's home but were said to have encouraged the abuse or helped in other ways.

Oakley told the jury: "During the course of this case, you may hear references to unconventional sexual practices, such as 'swinging' and 'sleep fetishes' and other 'kinks'.

"It may be suggested that the imagery you see is posed, and that [the victim] is in fact only pretending to be asleep or unconscious as part of a fantasy role play with her husband.

"The prosecution says that is a smokescreen; what these men did was not participation in unconventional but consensual sexual practices.

"It was rape and sexual assault, pure and simple."

Oakley gave an example of a message from Stewart to the husband sent within hours of Stewart allegedly raping the victim in September 2025.

"Mate, have had a bad feeling about it all day," she read.

"Delete all images from your phone etc as it's too risky. Remember what happened to the guy in France.

"Delete me from your phone and life. If she caught you out, it would be a whole lot of trouble and end of your marriage and ruin your life."

Oakley told the jury: "As you will no doubt remember, 'the guy in France', the man in France, who had been raping his wife, a lady by the name of Gisele Pelicot."

The jury heard the husband in the Stockport area case, after pleading guilty, had given an account of his actions and would appear as a witness.

He told prosecutors he had begun abusing his wife in the early 2000s.

Initially, he would record himself abusing her while she was unaware and kept the images "for himself".

However, he soon progressed to sharing images on online chatrooms with other "like-minded" men.

Oakley said in a "sick and perverted twist" he would sometimes pretend to be his wife in conversations online, but said that had stopped fairly "early on".

The jury heard the investigation into the abuse began after a team of undercover investigative journalists infiltrated a channel on the encrypted messaging service Telegram in October 2025.

The channel appeared to involve men sharing images of apparently unconscious women being raped and sexually assaulted.

One user in particular, Oakley said, was claiming he had been drugging and raping his wife and was inviting others to join in - while also sharing images of her.

The user was linked to a phone number registered to the husband, enabling Greater Manchester Police to obtain a warrant to search his address.

Oakley said when the contents of his phone were downloaded, material was found in a secure folder titled "visits", which also had messaging apps he had used to contact other defendants.

She said the jury would only be given a selection of the files involved, but the police had viewed every single one "line-by-line".

The husband has pleaded guilty to 62 offences including rape, adminstering a substance with intent, sharing intimate images and assault by penetration.

Keith Fotheringham, 59, from Dundee in Scotland; Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport; Graham Brougham, 74, from Northwich in Cheshire, and Karl Lindsay, 55, from Taunton in Somerset, have also pleaded guilty to a number of offences.

Indie rock band Courteeners are the latest headlining act to be announced for a series of concerts in south Shropshire.

The band have been together for 20 years, and this year released a new best-of compilation album called God Bless The Band, which they will perform in Ludlow.

They are currently travelling around the country on a tour of the same name.

The greatest hits record features songs from each of their seven albums, which frontman and songwriter Liam Fray said made him reminisce .

The concerts in Ludlow began in 2023, with 50,000 people visiting this year over two weekends, to see the likes of Snow Patrol, Paul Weller, The Human League, Tom Grennan, The Streets, Rick Astley, Richard Ashcroft and Scissor Sisters.

articles.title: A father left one daughter his $3.2 million Maryland trust; after he died at 95, her two sisters found handwritten Farsi notes and challenged the inheritance, and a court has now ordered a new trial
articles.summary: A Maryland appeals court has ordered a new trial in a major legal dispute between three sisters over their late father's $3.2 million trust fund.
articles.body: A Maryland appeals court has ordered a new trial in a major legal dispute between three sisters over their late father's $3.2 million trust fund. The court found that trial judges had wrongly blocked important handwriting evidence from being presented. In an opinion issued in October 2026, the Appellate Court of Maryland overturned an earlier ruling that had given one daughter sole control of the estate. The appeals court found that mistakes in the legal process had prevented the other two sisters from having a fair chance to challenge their father's estate documents. The dispute involves the estate of an elderly father who died at the age of 95, leaving behind a trust worth several million dollars.Disputed trust and handwritten notesThe legal dispute began after the father's death, when two of his daughters discovered that his main estate planning document, the S.K. Amini Trust of Maryland, named their third sister as the only main beneficiary and trustee. While looking through family records, the two excluded sisters found documents containing handwritten notes in Farsi, the modern Persian language spoken in Iran. One of the sisters recognised the handwriting on an important Farsi note and claimed it belonged not to their father, but to the sister who had been named the only beneficiary. A certified English translation of the Farsi note was presented during the trial. It was used to support claims that the favoured daughter had improperly influenced their elderly father or had directly helped control his estate plans while managing his personal and medical affairs. The two sisters later filed a lawsuit. They accused their sibling of using undue influence and wrongfully interfering with their expected inheritance. They also asked the court to cancel the trust and divide the estate equally among all three daughters.Procedural missteps and expert evidenceThe main issue in the appeals court's decision was the trial judge's refusal to allow a qualified handwriting expert hired by the two challenging sisters to testify. During the original circuit court proceedings, the judge stopped the expert from giving evidence about whether the Farsi handwriting was genuine. The judge based this decision on missed discovery deadlines and court scheduling rules. However, the Appellate Court of Maryland found that the lower court had made a serious error by excluding the handwriting expert. This was especially concerning because the judge had allowed more flexibility with the court schedule for the main legal witness supporting the sister defending the trust. According to court filings, the lawyer who prepared the trust documents, Kooresh Sobhani, was allowed to give evidence remotely despite earlier objections and legal requests to prevent it. Sobhani speaks both English and Farsi fluently. He told the court that he communicated with the father in both languages and said the elderly man was alert, mentally capable, and free from pressure or improper influence when he signed the trust documents. The appeals court found that blocking the handwriting expert's testimony seriously harmed the two sisters' ability to support their claims of wrongful interference and undue influence.Burden of proof and legal standardsAlong with reviewing the evidence, the appeals court also looked at the legal rules for claims involving intentional interference with an expected inheritance under Maryland law. The judges explained the difference between the legal standards used in general civil cases and the stronger level of proof needed to establish undue influence. Writing for the appeals panel, the court explained that ordinary claims involving financial interference usually require a preponderance of the evidence. This means showing that a claim is more likely to be true than not. However, claims that someone wrongly interfered with an inheritance through undue influence require clear, satisfactory, and convincing evidence. The court concluded that the circuit court had made conflicting decisions about legal procedures. These decisions limited the sisters' ability to meet the required standard of proof. As a result, the original judgment could not remain in place.Case remanded for fresh proceedingsThe appeals court officially cancelled the circuit court's judgment and sent the case back to the local trial court for a completely new trial. The decision reopens the dispute over the $3.2 million trust. It gives all three sisters another opportunity to present their evidence. This includes the disputed Farsi notes, expert handwriting analysis, and witness testimony about what their late father truly wanted for his estate. articles.title: In 2000, a North Carolina sculptor began building a small woodland cabin on his 14-acre property; it grew into a 60-foot, four-storey castle that later attracted photographers despite years of abandonment
articles.summary: What began as a quiet plan for a simple retreat in the North Carolina woods eventually became something far more ambitious.
articles.body: What began as a quiet plan for a simple retreat in the North Carolina woods eventually became something far more ambitious. On 14 acres in Rougemont, Person County, sculptor Robert Mihaly started building himself a small cabin in 2000. More than two decades later, that modest project had transformed into a 60-foot, four-storey structure with the look and feel of a fairytale castle.From woodland cabin to towering castleMihaly, a self-taught artist based in Durham, initially envisioned the property as a secluded place where he could live and work. But the construction kept expanding, floor by floor and room by room, until the little cabin had become Castle Mont Rouge.According to ABC11, the finished structure covers more than 2,000 square feet and rises over four levels. Mihaly lived there for several years before eventually leaving the property. Without its creator living there, the unusual building developed a life of its own.Mystery draws curious visitorsCastle Mont Rouge sat largely abandoned for years, adding an air of mystery to the property. Its secluded location and unusual architecture attracted curious visitors, some of whom left graffiti behind or caused damage.The castle's unfinished and weathered appearance also made it appealing to people looking for something outside the usual locations for creative projects. ABC11 reported that, with Mihaly's permission, the property has been used for music videos as well as wedding and engagement photography.The site has even attracted ghost hunters and people interested in its archaeological possibilities, further adding to its unusual reputation.A new chapter for Castle Mont RougeThe castle's story took another turn when Mihaly decided to return to the project. He began working on the property again with plans to transform it into an event destination and vineyard.His ambitions for the castle became particularly personal. He hoped to have the property ready for his daughter's 16th birthday, giving the decades-long construction project a deadline and a family milestone to work toward.But the attempt to turn the castle into a business became complicated by a relationship that eventually ended in court.A business deal turns into a legal fightAccording to CBS 17, Mihaly met Julie Seel through Match.com in 2023. The relationship moved quickly, and the pair soon became involved in plans to develop Castle Mont Rouge as an event venue.Seel provided financing for the venture, including a $250,000 loan to a company connected with the project. The arrangement was based on an informal agreement involving the property and proposed ownership.When the relationship broke down, however, so did the business partnership. Mihaly accused Seel of attempting to gain control of his property through the relationship, while Seel alleged that Mihaly had sought her financial resources to help complete the castle.The fairytale gets complicatedAfter a two-year legal dispute, a Durham County Superior Court judge dismissed both sides' claims following two days of testimony, CBS 17 reported.The court battle left both parties facing financial and personal consequences, while Castle Mont Rouge remained at the centre of the dispute.For Mihaly, however, the strange journey of his creation continues. What started as a small cabin has survived abandonment, vandalism, creative productions and a bitter legal battle. Its next chapter may finally be the one its creator imagined all those years ago, a castle filled with people rather than mystery.Image Courtesy: CBS 17You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: An electricity bill is rarely something most households look forward to receiving, but for an 85-year-old pensioner in South Australia, correspondence
articles.body: An electricity bill is rarely something most households look forward to receiving, but for an 85-year-old pensioner in South Australia, correspondence from his former energy provider brought a particularly confusing turn of events. After leaving ENGIE over rising electricity costs, Bill Nedeff was informed that the company had discovered he had been overcharged by more than $10,000. He was asked to claim the money back. However, the figures began changing, and the credit eventually turned into a debt. By August 2025, Nedeff was being told he owed the company money, with debt collectors also contacting him. It took months of questioning before ENGIE acknowledged its mistake.How an Australian pensioner's $10,763 electricity refund became a debtNedeff's dealings with ENGIE had already ended when the company contacted him in June 2025. The pensioner, who lives with his wife at Encounter Bay, south of Adelaide, had switched providers after becoming increasingly concerned about the cost of his electricity bills. ENGIE said an error had been identified in his account, resulting in an overcharge of $10,763.27, as reported by ABC News.The company apologised and instructed him to request a refund. But the amount did not remain unchanged for long. By August, ENGIE had reversed its position altogether, informing Nedeff that he owed it $1,120. Letters from a debt collection agency followed, adding another complication to what had started as a request for a refund.The changing figures left Nedeff struggling to understand his account. He told ABC's 7.30, "I was having a few sleepless nights over it and that wouldn't be just, say, tonight and tomorrow night, it was over a number of weeks.”Australian family challenges ENGIE after reviewing years of electricity billsNedeff's daughter, Fiona Han, became involved as the family tried to establish where the figures had come from. They approached the South Australian Energy and Water Ombudsman, seeking an explanation for the contradictory statements. By November 17, the amount ENGIE claimed was outstanding had fallen from $1,120 to $280.Although Nedeff considered settling the smaller amount, Han was reluctant to accept the revised bill without a proper breakdown. She had seen the original letter acknowledging the overcharge and believed the company needed to explain how an account that had been in credit could suddenly become a debt. The family also began examining years of electricity statements, many of which had been kept in shoeboxes.Reportedly, Nedeff had installed 30 solar panels on his roof, making the growing charges difficult for the family to reconcile. According to the bills they examined, his peak electricity rate had risen from 43 cents per kilowatt-hour in June 2022 to 75 cents the following month. By 2024-25, it had reached 83 cents per kilowatt-hour, before he left ENGIE.On December 9, 2025, the company finally confirmed that Nedeff did not owe it anything. Instead, its revised calculations showed that he had been overcharged by $2,470. The amount was considerably lower than the original credit of $10,763.ENGIE faces further scrutiny over billing errors and customer complaintsIn its response to ABC's 7.30, ENGIE attributed the problem to mistakes made during a manual adjustment of Nedeff's account."We have found an agent has made manual data entry errors in the process, resulting in incorrect bill amounts being sent to Mr Nedeff and one other ENGIE customer. We're very sorry for the confusion this caused and are working with the ombudsman and customers to refund the correct amount and resolve this issue."ENGIE acknowledged that the error had caused confusion and apologised. It also said it was working with the relevant customers and the ombudsman to arrange the correct refunds and settle the matter. The incident came amid wider questions about the retailer's billing practices in South Australia. In August 2025, ENGIE had been required to correct electricity bills for as many as 3,000 customers after acknowledging that they had been overcharged.Reportedly, the company was also facing regulatory scrutiny elsewhere. In late November 2025, Victoria's Essential Services Commission fined ENGIE $1.2 million following an investigation into delays in responding to customer complaints about billing.ENGIE separately acknowledged, "We've made meaningful changes to staffing, training and key customer processes and seen a significant improvement in service performance as a result.”Electricity rate increases raised further questionsFor Han, the dispute was not limited to the incorrect refund and the debt collection letters. Her examination of the household's older bills suggested that her parents had been paying substantially higher electricity rates for several years.South Australian Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis also criticised the way the company had handled Nedeff's account. He said the errors risked undermining customers' confidence in electricity retailers, particularly when people could no longer be certain that the amounts on their bills were accurate.Koutsantonis argued that customers should not have to question every charge simply to establish whether they were being billed correctly. He also raised concerns about the commercial incentives of energy retailers, suggesting that customer service was not always receiving the attention it required.Experts call for stronger protections against the electricity market's 'loyalty tax'Ron Ben-David, a former chair of Victoria's Essential Services Commission who now works at Monash University Business School, described the practice as a 'loyalty tax'. His argument is that customers who rarely compare electricity plans can gradually end up paying higher rates, sometimes without realising how far their costs have moved from the available market offers. Figures from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission's 2025 Electricity Inquiry Report found that 73.3% of Australian households were not on the best available electricity deal.Ben-David has argued for a consumer duty that would require energy retailers to consider customers' interests when offering and managing contracts. Rather than leaving households to navigate an increasingly complicated market, companies would have a greater responsibility to identify plans suited to individual circumstances.For Nedeff, the dispute eventually ended with ENGIE acknowledging that he had been overcharged, rather than owing the company money. But the months between the original refund letter and the final correction involved changing bills, repeated requests for explanations and contact from debt collectors.Disclaimer: This article is based on information publicly available online. The Times of India has not independently verified the claims, billing figures or circumstances mentioned. The information should not be interpreted as an official statement from ENGIE or the individuals involved.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Police attacked with fireworks and bottles ahead of cup semi-final
articles.summary: The disorder happened on Curtis Avenue ahead of the Rangers v Aberdeen match at Hampden on Saturday.
articles.body:
Police Scotland officers were attacked with fireworks and glass bottles ahead of the Rangers v Aberdeen league cup semi-final.

The disorder, which also involved "other missiles", happened on Curtis Avenue before the game at Hampden on Saturday.

Several officers were assaulted during the "targeted" incident while two fans were also hurt but did not require medical attention.

The force said a man was also arrested in a separate incident outside the stadium in in connection with an assault.

Supt Paul Douglas said: "This violence is disgraceful and will not be tolerated.

"Being assaulted is not part of the job and it's extremely fortunate they were not seriously injured.

"Those involved should be in no doubt that they will be identified and arrested."

He added inquiries were ongoing to trace those responsible and confirmed officers would work closely with both clubs.

Douglas said: "We recognise that only a small percentage of fans behave in such a way and cause disorder, but I would encourage all fans to take personal responsibility for their conduct."

He asked anyone with information to contact Police Scotland .

Officers also responded to a number of incidents on Sunday during the second semi-final, between Edinburgh rivals Hearts and Hibernian.

Four men, aged between 24 and 37, were arrested during the match for offences including threatening and abusive behaviour and possession of pyrotechnics.

They were released on an undertaking and will appear before Glasgow Sheriff Court at a later date.

Police said another man was charged and reported to the fiscal for alleged vandalism in the national stadium.

Two men also received police warnings for threatening and abusive behaviour.

A 28-year-old man was later arrested and charged outside the stadium for similar offences and will be reported to the fiscal.

Another man was issued with a recorded police warning for threatening and abusive behaviour.

The force also confirmed three men and a woman will be reported to the fiscal for pyrotechnic offences, as well as threatening and abusive behaviour.

Rangers beat Aberdeen 1-0 after a late strike by Ryan Nadeeri to secure their place in the final.

Derek McInnes' side will face Hibs at Hampden on 13 December, after they came from behind to beat Hearts 2-1 .

articles.title: ‘Where did 300,000 children go?’: YouTuber Nick Shirley targets US NGOs over alleged trafficking network
articles.summary: YouTuber Nick Shirley has accused several US non-governmental organizations (NGOs) of being involved in the trafficking of more than 300,000 children
articles.body: YouTuber Nick Shirley has accused several US non-governmental organizations (NGOs) of being involved in the trafficking of more than 300,000 children across the country. In a new investigative video, the YouTuber claimed that these groups received millions of dollars in government funding while children went missing from the system. He also questioned what happened to children who crossed the US border in recent years. Shirley called the alleged operation the "largest government-funded human trafficking ring in history." However, his claims have not been independently established.Nick Shirley Questions Where Thousands of Migrant Children Went After Entering the USIn a post on X, YouTuber Shirley shared his allegations and pointed to the amount of public money he believes went to the organizations involved."Your tax dollars trafficked over 300,000 children across the United States while NGOs enriched themselves with millions of dollars," he wrote.He also claimed that one organization received around $895 million to move children across the country, while others received more than $100 million. However, he did not establish in his post that these payments were used for human trafficking.In the video, Shirley spoke about a 17-year-old girl who reportedly crossed the US border illegally in 2023. He questioned what had happened to children who entered the country during those years and why their current whereabouts were unclear.He also interviewed a woman who was introduced as a former contract specialist at the US General Services Administration (GSA). She said the children were meant to be placed with sponsors. However, the discussion raised questions about who those sponsors were and what information was available about the children after their release.Shirley then approached several officials to ask about the children. According to the footage, the people he questioned said they did not know where the children were.One organization he named was VisionQuest, a Tucson-based group that provides services to children and families. Shirley questioned its staff about the government funding it had received and tried to get answers about its work. However, he did not receive a response from the employees he approached.Federal records do confirm that VisionQuest received government funding. According to the US government's USAspending website, the organization had a grant worth around $16.8 million for services under the Unaccompanied Alien Children Program between May 2023 and October 2026. This funding record does not establish Shirley's allegation of human trafficking.Nick Shirley Visits More NGOs After Making Claims About Missing ChildrenVisionQuest was not the only organization Shirley approached. He also visited the Jewish Family & Children's Service of Southern Arizona and asked its staff about children who had crossed the border between 2021 and 2024.One employee did not provide the information he was seeking and said someone would contact him later. Shirley then visited another organization and asked similar questions. The footage showed staff members unable to give him details about the children's whereabouts.The video has brought attention to the way the US government tracks and places unaccompanied migrant children with sponsors. However, questions about record-keeping and the movement of children do not by themselves prove that NGOs were involved in trafficking.This is not the first time Shirley has faced attention over claims involving government-funded organizations. In December 2025, he released a video accusing several Somali-run childcare centers in Minnesota of receiving public money without providing proper daycare services.According to NPR, his video led to fresh scrutiny of the centers and prompted state and federal officials to look into the allegations. However, the Minnesota Department of Children, Youth, and Families said in January 2026 that nine centers it checked were operating as expected. CBS News also reported that its review found no recorded evidence of fraud at the centers it examined.President Donald Trump later praised Shirley for his Minnesota daycare video, according to CBS News. His latest investigation now raises a different set of questions about federal funding and the care of migrant children. The allegations against the NGOs, however, still need independent evidence and official findings.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1889, a Texas family settled on ranchland along the Colorado River; 137 years later, more than 3,100 acres have become a new state park, with trails opening to visitors as restoration and development continue
articles.summary: In 1889, John Fletcher and Mattie Lou Vann settled on a piece of ranchland along the Colorado River in Central Texas.
articles.body: In 1889, John Fletcher and Mattie Lou Vann settled on a piece of ranchland along the Colorado River in Central Texas. The couple raised seven children there, and generations of their family continued to use the property for ranching, cutting cedar and operating a fishing camp.More than 137 years later, land that includes part of the family's former ranch has become Post Oak Ridge State Park. The 3,118-acre property opened for independent day visits on September 24, 2026, giving the public access to a landscape of rolling hills, wooded ridges, limestone cliffs and river overlooks. The park is still being developed, with camping facilities and additional visitor amenities expected around 2029, according to the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD).From a family ranch in 1889 to a state park in 2026The history of Post Oak Ridge stretches back to 1889, when John Fletcher and Mattie Lou Vann established their home on the land. Their seven children and later generations maintained a connection to the property, using it for cattle ranching, cedar cutting and recreational fishing.In January 2025, Texas began acquiring land for the new state park, including property owned by descendants of the Vann family. The acquisitions eventually brought 3,118 acres under state ownership, creating one of the newest additions to Texas' public park system.The property was attractive to conservation officials because of its location along the Colorado River, directly across from Colorado Bend State Park. Park superintendent Kacey Sloan told local broadcaster 25 News KXXV that the land's position within the neighbouring park's viewshed was an important reason for the state's interest.The acquisition has also brought land with a long family and agricultural history into public ownership, where its natural features and cultural heritage can be protected while visitors gain access to the area.What makes the 3,118-acre property special?Post Oak Ridge stretches across parts of Burnet and Lampasas counties in Central Texas. Its landscape includes spring-fed creeks, limestone bluffs, canyons, post oak woodlands and scenic overlooks of the Colorado River.The park takes its name from the post oak trees found along its ridges. These woodlands, together with the river bluffs and creeks, form part of an ecologically diverse landscape that Texas Parks and Wildlife intends to protect as visitor facilities are developed.The property also sits close to Colorado Bend State Park, creating opportunities to protect neighbouring natural landscapes while expanding public access to the region.According to TPWD, natural and cultural research and restoration are continuing alongside development work. The agency intends to design facilities around the sensitive habitats rather than significantly altering the landscape.What visitors can explore at Post Oak Ridge todayAlthough the land was acquired in 2025, September 24, 2026, marked an important change in public access. Before that, visitors could participate in organised activities such as guided hikes, birdwatching, educational programmes and public hunts.The September opening introduced independent day visits, allowing people to explore designated trails without joining a guided group.The park currently offers around four miles of hiking trails, scenic overlooks, an accessible trail and picnic area, a gravel access road and basic restroom facilities.However, it remains a developing park rather than a fully equipped recreation destination. Visitors must reserve their day passes in advance. There is no drinking water or electricity available, mobile phone coverage is limited, and access is restricted to designated trails.Overnight camping and direct recreational access to the river are not yet part of the regular day-use facilities.How a $1 billion conservation fund is helping develop the parkPost Oak Ridge is among the first new Texas state parks being developed using interest generated by the Centennial Parks Conservation Fund.Texas voters approved the creation of the $1 billion fund in 2023 to support the acquisition and development of new state parks. The fund is intended to provide long-term financial support as population growth increases demand for public recreation areas.Under the state's constitutional framework, interest earned on money credited to the fund is reserved for creating and improving state parks.Post Oak Ridge is an early example of that initiative. The state began acquiring the property in 2025, expanded public access in September 2026 and plans to introduce more substantial facilities over the coming years.What will change by 2029?Texas Parks and Wildlife expects Post Oak Ridge to reach its next major development stage around 2029, approximately four years after the initial land acquisition.Plans include improved roads, utilities, a park headquarters, RV sites, overnight camping facilities, additional trails and eventual river access.Sloan told 25 News KXXV that developing these facilities is comparable to building a small city within the park, with substantial infrastructure required even when the finished development is intended to blend into its surroundings.The department has also involved local communities in planning the park. Four public meetings and two surveys were conducted to gather views on recreation, environmental protection, road access, cultural history and future facilities.For now, Post Oak Ridge offers visitors a chance to explore former ranchland while work continues on its transformation into a fully developed state park. The land's journey, from a family settlement established in 1889 to a publicly accessible park in 2026, is now part of the region's conservation history.You use AI every day. articles.title: Row erupts after Scottish govt sends IT contract to Bengaluru to administer welfare payment
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from London: The Scottish National Party, which governs Scotland, has come under fire from opposition ministers for handing a £35.4
articles.body: TOI correspondent from London: The Scottish National Party, which governs Scotland, has come under fire from opposition ministers for handing a £35.4 million (almost Rs 450 crore) contract to an IT services company in Bengaluru.Under the contract, Mphasis will manage and maintain Scotland’s benefits management platform that delivers welfare benefits to around two million citizens across Scotland.Scotland first minister John Swinney has just returned from a trade mission to India where he was meant to be finding opportunities to support jobs and prosperity across Scotland, so news that he has instead sent lucrative work to India has sparked fiery criticism back home.Scottish Labour’s social justice spokesman, Mark Griffin, told the “Scottish Mail on Sunday”: “We should be using public contracts like this to boost local business and the Scottish economy and create jobs in Scotland. All too often, under SNP, good work has flowed overseas. SNP ministers should explain why this decision was made.”Shadow secretary of state for Scotland Harriet Cross posted on X: “They send millions to India to help administer their ballooning benefits system. This is taxpayers’ money. And they’re sending it abroad.”“Our ongoing relationship with Social Security Scotland allows us to support one of the country’s most critical public service platforms, and our commitment is to maintain continuity, improve operational efficiency and deliver meaningful outcomes for individuals and families across Scotland. The project aligns with our broader public sector focus; supporting govt organisations in running secure, reliable and future-ready digital services,” said Ashish Devalekar, executive vice-president and head of Europe, Mphasis.A Social Security Scotland spokesperson told TOI: “Contracts are awarded in line with the Scottish govt’s procurement guidelines, which state that bids are to be treated equally, regardless of the location. This ensures that we award contracts to the bidder offering the best overall value. Investment in technology ensures we are future proof and adaptable to changing demands for our payments.”Sources in the Scottish govt told TOI that the platform “requires highly specialised expertise in a niche technology area with a relatively small number of suppliers globally able to demonstrate the scale, experience and capability required”.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Louisiana woman paid $32,500 for a wooden river barrier to protect her $109,000 home, but it failed in a flood and her house shifted; a court has now awarded her nearly $450,000 after removing her share of blame
articles.summary: A riverfront home can face years of damage from erosion and moving water, making protective structures an important investment for homeowners.
articles.body: A riverfront home can face years of damage from erosion and moving water, making protective structures an important investment for homeowners. But when a barrier built to safeguard a property fails during a flood, the consequences can extend far beyond the cost of replacing it. One Louisiana homeowner experienced this after a wooden river barrier collapsed, leaving her house structurally compromised and requiring hundreds of thousands of dollars in repairs.The Louisiana Court of Appeal, Third Circuit, addressed the dispute in its October 30, 2026, decision in Elizabeth D. Molbert v. Kenko Bulkhead & Marine Services, LLC, et al., available on Justia. The court examined the contractor's responsibility for the failed construction, the homeowner's share of fault and the extent of the contractor's insurance coverage. It ultimately removed the homeowner's share of responsibility, increased her mental anguish compensation and revised the damages awarded, bringing her total recovery to $448,431.34.A $32,500 bulkhead was built to protect the riverfront propertyElizabeth Molbert purchased her home along the west fork of the Calcasieu River in 2009 for $109,000. Several years later, concerned about erosion caused by the river's moving water, she hired Kenko Bulkhead & Marine Services LLC to construct a 130-foot wooden bulkhead. The structure, completed in June 2016, cost $32,500. Its purpose was to prevent the riverbank from eroding and protect the house from the effects of the moving water.However, the bulkhead failed during a flood in May 2017. Molbert subsequently discovered that the consequences extended beyond the damaged river barrier. Because Kenko had connected the original wooden bulkhead to a piling supporting the house, the structure's failure caused the house to shift. Molbert filed a claim under her flood insurance policy with Liberty Mutual. An appraisal determined that her losses exceeded the policy limit, and the insurer paid her $165,000. She also replaced the failed wooden structure with an engineered steel bulkhead, which cost $167,058.59. Repairs to her house added another $266,372.75 to her expenses.Homeowner sued contractor over defective constructionIn March 2018, Molbert filed a damages lawsuit against Kenko and its insurer, Travelers Property Casualty Company of America. She alleged that defective construction of the bulkhead had caused the damage to her property. She later amended her lawsuit to include Kenko's owners, Kenneth Cooley and Glenn Beier. Among her allegations was that the two men had assured her they were licensed contractors and legally qualified to perform the work, although they did not have the required licences.The case went to a jury trial in September 2024. The jury assigned 75% of the responsibility for the damages to Kenko, Cooley and Beier collectively, while finding Molbert 25% at fault. It awarded her $266,372.75 for damage to the house, $167,058.59 for the bulkhead and shoreline, $2,500 for loss of enjoyment of life and $7,500 for mental anguish. After reducing the award to account for her 25% share of fault, her recovery was calculated at $332,573.50. The trial court subsequently dismissed the claims against Cooley and Beier in their individual capacities. The homeowner, contractor and insurer all appealed.Appeals court examined licensing and insurance coverageA central issue before the appeals court was whether Travelers could avoid covering the damages under exclusions in its commercial general liability policy. The insurer argued that the policy's breach-of-contract exclusion applied because the dispute arose from the agreement to construct the bulkhead. However, the appeals court found that the exclusion did not prevent coverage because Kenko did not hold the required licences to perform the contracted work. Under Louisiana law, a construction contract entered into in violation of licensing requirements can be considered an absolute nullity.The judges also examined the policy's work-product exclusion. They ruled that Travelers' policy excluded the $167,058.59 cost of repairing and replacing the defective bulkhead itself. The court also clarified that the jury's award under the combined 'shoreline/bulkhead' category represented bulkhead replacement costs alone, as Molbert had not restored the shoreline. However, the damage to Molbert's house was covered under the policy's products-completed operations hazard provision because it involved damage to other property after the construction work had been completed. The policy did not cover the mental anguish award, a finding by the trial court that remained undisturbed on appeal. Thus, although Molbert's total damages award increased to $448,431.34, Travelers' coverage did not extend to the entire amount.The court also rejected Kenko's argument that the homeowner's $165,000 flood insurance payment should be deducted from her recovery. It explained that Molbert remained entitled to pursue the unpaid portion of her damages, although she would have to reimburse Liberty Mutual in accordance with the policy's subrogation clause.Court removes homeowner's fault and increases compensationOne of the most significant findings concerned the jury's decision to hold Molbert 25% responsible for the damage. The appeals court found that the evidence overwhelmingly established that the bulkhead failed because of improper design and construction. Experts testified that the structure lacked necessary rock protection, proper soil compaction and sufficient height. These deficiencies contributed to the failure, and none of the experts attributed fault to Molbert.The contractor had also argued that she should have removed a temporary stabilisation beam attached to the house piling. However, the court said she was a homeowner who had hired marine construction professionals and could not reasonably have been expected to understand the structural risks. It therefore removed her share of fault entirely. The court also increased her mental anguish award from $7,500 to $15,000. It considered her financial difficulties, including withdrawing retirement savings, taking additional jobs and delaying retirement to pay for the repairs. However, it removed the separate $2,500 award for loss of enjoyment of life, finding insufficient evidence to support such compensation without physical injury.The final judgment awarded Molbert $266,372.75 for damage to her home, $167,058.59 for replacement of the bulkhead and $15,000 for mental anguish, bringing her total damages award to $448,431.34. The court also ordered Kenko and Travelers to bear 100% of the trial court costs, expert witness fees and transcript costs.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A US internet provider was sued by music companies over songs shared by its customers; the Supreme Court ruled on when an internet company can be held responsible for copyright infringement
articles.summary: A US Supreme Court ruling has clarified when an internet service provider can be held responsible for copyright violations committed by its customers.
articles.body: A US Supreme Court ruling has clarified when an internet service provider can be held responsible for copyright violations committed by its customers. The case involved Cox Communications, which faced a lawsuit from Sony Music Entertainment and other record companies over songs allegedly shared illegally through its internet connections. The music companies argued that Cox should be held accountable because it continued providing services to subscribers despite receiving repeated piracy complaints. The court disagreed, ruling that simply knowing about copyright infringement does not automatically make an internet provider legally responsible.Supreme Court ruling limits internet providers' liability for music piracyOn March 25, 2026, the US Supreme Court delivered its decision in Cox Communications, Inc. v. Sony Music Entertainment. It ruled that an internet provider cannot be held responsible for copyright infringement simply because it knows that some customers are using its services to share protected material illegally.The court said that a company must intend for its service to be used for copyright infringement before it can be held liable for contributing to that activity. This could happen if a business actively encourages illegal sharing or provides a service specifically designed to support copyright violations.Justice Clarence Thomas delivered the opinion of the court. The decision was unanimous in its outcome, although Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson agreed with the judgment separately.The ruling overturned the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals' earlier decision that had found Cox liable for contributory copyright infringement. The Supreme Court's official opinion explained that providing an internet connection to someone who later breaks copyright law does not, by itself, establish the provider's responsibility.How Sony Music built its case against Cox CommunicationsThe dispute began with record companies trying to address the widespread sharing of copyrighted music online. Sony Music Entertainment and other companies hired MarkMonitor, a firm that used monitoring software to identify songs being uploaded and downloaded without permission.The software traced suspected activity to IP addresses, which could then be linked to internet service providers. These providers received notices identifying connections associated with possible copyright violations.According to the Supreme Court judgment, Cox received 163,148 infringement notices over roughly 2 years. Sony argued that the company had enough information to identify repeat offenders but continued allowing many of them to use its network.The music companies maintained that Cox's approach allowed piracy to continue and that the provider benefited financially by retaining subscribers who repeatedly violated copyright rules.Cox, however, questioned whether an IP address could reliably identify the person responsible. An internet connection might be shared by several people in a household, university accommodation or public establishment. Disconnecting an entire account could therefore affect customers who had nothing to do with the alleged infringement.Cox's warning system became a central part of the disputeCox said it already had procedures for dealing with copyright complaints. Its system involved sending warnings to subscribers after receiving repeated notices and taking stronger action if the activity continued.Under the policy, a second infringement notice could trigger a warning. Further complaints could result in temporary suspension of internet access until the subscriber responded. Continued reports could lead to additional suspensions and telephone warnings. After 13 notices, Cox could terminate the account.The company also prohibited customers from using its services to distribute copyrighted material without permission.Sony questioned whether Cox genuinely enforced these rules. The record companies pointed out that the provider had terminated only 32 subscribers for copyright infringement during the period examined in the case.They also referred to internal company communications suggesting that Cox was reluctant to lose paying customers. The music companies argued that its financial interests had influenced how strictly it dealt with repeat offenders.Cox disputed this interpretation and maintained that its system had stopped 98% of the identified infringement.A $1 billion damages award brought the dispute to the Supreme CourtSony and the other record companies filed their lawsuit in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia. They argued that Cox was responsible for both contributing to copyright infringement and benefiting financially from it.In 2019, a jury found the company liable under both claims and awarded the music companies $1 billion in statutory damages.Cox appealed the decision. The Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the finding of contributory liability but rejected the separate claim of vicarious liability, which concerns situations where a company benefits from infringement and has the ability to supervise the person responsible.The appeals court also set aside the original damages award and sent the case back for further consideration of the amount.Cox then took the contributory liability issue to the Supreme Court. The justices agreed to examine whether the company could be held responsible simply for continuing to provide internet access to subscribers accused of piracy.Why the court distinguished internet access from piracy softwareThe Supreme Court relied on earlier decisions to explain why businesses should not automatically be held responsible for every illegal use of their products or services.One important example was the 1984 Sony Betamax case. At the time, the court ruled that selling video recording equipment did not make a manufacturer responsible for copyright violations committed by customers. The equipment had substantial lawful uses, even though some people could use it to make unauthorised copies.The justices also considered the 2005 Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Studios Inc. v. Grokster Ltd. decision. That case involved file-sharing software companies accused of actively encouraging users to obtain copyrighted material illegally.The court found an important difference between those circumstances and Cox's business. Unlike software promoted for illegal file-sharing, Cox provided ordinary internet access that customers used for countless legitimate purposes, including education, work, communication and entertainment.The court also rejected the suggestion that the Digital Millennium Copyright Act automatically made internet providers liable if they failed to terminate every subscriber accused of repeated infringement.Separate opinion highlights concerns about copyright protectionAlthough all nine justices agreed with the final outcome, Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, wrote a separate opinion.Sotomayor questioned whether contributory copyright liability should be limited to the two categories identified by the majority. She argued that other legal principles, including aiding and abetting, could also apply when a company helps someone commit infringement.She also raised concerns about how the ruling could affect incentives for internet providers to deal with repeat offenders.Nevertheless, she agreed that the evidence against Cox was insufficient to establish liability in this case. The Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit's decision on contributory infringement and returned the case for further proceedings.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Apple News maintains left-leaning tilt under new CEO John Ternus, conservative watchdog group says
articles.summary: The Media Research Center says Apple News promoted only 11 stories from right-leaning outlets out of 504 published in October's first 27 days.
articles.body: Apple News continues to push content from left-leaning news organizations and frame information about President Donald Trump in a negative light, according to studies conducted by the Media Research Center (MRC). The MRC, a conservative media watchdog, previously found Apple News took a "decidedly leftist turn" after comparing content during the final month of former CEO Tim Cook’s tenure to the first month after new CEO John Ternus took control on Sept 1. The group then monitored Apple News through October and found the news aggregator continued to largely promote left-leaning outlets in the lead up to midterm elections. Apple News promoted only 11 stories from right-leaning outlets out of a total of 504 published stories through the first 27 days of October, according to the MRC. More than two out of every three stories came from a publication that media bias rating site AllSides considers left-leaning, as 67.3% were from liberal outlets and only 2% came from right-leaning outlets. APPLE, GOOGLE NEWS ALGORITHMS SUPPRESSED NEGATIVE STORIES ON MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL EL-SAYED, STUDY SAYS The study found that Apple News, which comes preinstalled on every iPhone in America, was consistent with the percentage of stories from left-leaning outlets in each month since Ternus took control and noticed a slight bump in content from right-leaning outlets in his second month at the helm. However, nearly half of the content from right-leaning organizations was framed negatively against either the Trump administration or Republicans in general, according to the MRC. "For months the media has been claiming that Trump is on the ballot for the midterm elections. Given that Apple News has run only eleven stories from right-leaning outlets in October leading up to the election and nearly half were framed negatively against Trump, it’s apparent how Apple under John Ternus hopes the election turns out," MRC Free Speech America Dan Schneider told Fox News Digital. articles.title: After 28 years & 51,000-km trek around the world, Karl Bushby is back in UK
articles.summary: HULL (ENGLAND): Karl Bushby was taking the final steps Monday of his 28-year odyssey to walk around the world and return to his mother's home in northern
articles.body: HULL (ENGLAND): Karl Bushby was taking the final steps Monday of his 28-year odyssey to walk around the world and return to his mother's home in northern England. Bushby was surrounded by journalists as hundreds of people cheered his arrival at City Hall. "Sorry to keep you waiting," he joked. "Is that it, is it done?"Bushby was a 29-year-old ex-paratrooper when he walked from his home to a Royal Air Force base near Oxford and caught a flight to South America. He returned as a 57-year-old - softer, greyer and weathered, but far more worldly. "They say it takes a village but literally it took a world to get me here," Bushby said. "The kindness of strangers, so many, from individuals to nation states to get me back here today. I didn't do this alone. There was a big team. The biggest team. Earth."Bushby set out from Punta Arenas, Chile, on Nov 1, 1998, and has walked 50,000 kilometres across four continents and 30 countries to get home. He navigated shifting ice over the Bering Strait and swam across the Caspian Sea and English Channel to avoid taking a boat or plane - or any transport - to propel him forward.He had a thirst for adventure, but his mission only came into focus when his father, Keith, sent him a birthday card in the mid-90s. His dad, an army veteran himself, mentioned an argument among his fellow special forces troops about the possibility of walking from London to New York over the Bering land bridge, believed by some scientists to have been used by early humans to migrate from Asia to the Americas at a time of lower sea levels. Perilous jungles, scorching deserts and frozen tundra slowed him down, but bureaucratic red tape often brought his adventure to a halt for long periods.Bushby originally calculated the distance could be covered in about five years, but he knew that was unrealistic."You just dump a whole bucket full of reality on that," he said. "We suspected that it was 12 years plus. And the plus was a big plus. But never in our wildest dreams would we ever have imagined 28 years."He dodged war in the dangerous Darien Gap, the roadless and rugged jungle, rainforest and mountains between South and Central America in 2001, and was then jailed for 18 days after crossing a restricted border zone in Panama. After being airlifted to safety during the 90-km Bering Strait crossing in 2006 with American adventurer Dimitry Kieffer, they started again and faced a standoff with a polar bear, survived near-death plunges into freezing waters and almost lost all their supplies when their sleds plunged in the sea. After managing the rare crossing, the pair were jailed and faced deportation for entering Russia illegally.It took Bushby almost 10 years to make his way through Russia in fits and starts because of visa struggles and weather that allowed travel only a few months a year. When Russia denied him a visa in 2012, Bushby walked in protest from Los Angeles to the Russian embassy in Washington, DC, which eventually led to him getting the proper paperwork.Bushby planned to meet with family, including his son, Adam, whom he has only seen a few times over the journey. He was expected to meet his 12-year-old granddaughter for the first time. Then he was off to push his two-wheeled cart the final steps across Hull and reunite with his mother, Angela, whom he hadn't seen in a decade. "It's been a week of lasts," Bushby told the crowd."The last day in the tent. The last day on the road. After 28 years you couldn't ask for more than this. This is the last of the last few steps almost to my mother's house."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Nebraska couple faced the court-ordered sale of their family home over a commercial lease debt owed only by the husband; the state's Supreme Court vacated the sale decree because it wrongly covered the wife's share
articles.summary: A family home can become the centre of a legal dispute when a debt incurred by one spouse puts jointly owned property at risk.
articles.body: A family home can become the centre of a legal dispute when a debt incurred by one spouse puts jointly owned property at risk. In Nebraska, a couple faced the possible sale of their primary residence after a creditor sought to recover money owed by the husband under a commercial lease agreement. Although the debt was legally his alone, a lower court issued a decree ordering the sale of the entire property. In its October 30, 2026, decision in 11819 Miracle Hills Drive v. Ali, available on Justia, the Nebraska Supreme Court found that the order contained significant errors because the creditor's judgment lien applied only to the husband's undivided one-half interest, not his wife's share. The court vacated the decree and sent the case back for further proceedings.A commercial lease debt put the family home at riskThe dispute began when 11819 Miracle Hills Drive, LP, obtained a money judgment against Maman Lawan Ali over his breach of a commercial lease agreement. The judgment was against Ali individually, and his wife was not a party to the lease. The couple jointly owned their primary residence as joint tenants with right of survivorship. The property was also their family home, where they lived with their four children.After obtaining the judgment, Miracle Hills initiated a separate foreclosure action to enforce its lien against Ali's undivided one-half interest in the property. The creditor sought to recover the amount owed by selling the interest to which its judgment lien applied. Ali and his wife appeared without lawyers during the proceedings. Ali argued that the property was his family's residence and questioned how it could be foreclosed over a commercial lease debt.His wife raised a separate concern about the ownership arrangement. She maintained that the judgment was against her husband alone and that the creditor could not use his financial liability to interfere with her ownership interest in the home. She also argued that her share could not be divided or subjected to a judgment lien arising from a debt she had not incurred.Lower court ordered the sale of the entire propertyThe Douglas County District Court granted summary judgment in favour of Miracle Hills, finding no material factual disputes that prevented the foreclosure action from proceeding. It recognised the creditor's judgment lien and established that the mortgage lender's interest in the property had priority over the lien. The court then ordered that, unless the outstanding debt was paid within 20 days, the property would be sold.The decree identified the property by its legal description and common address, covering the couple's entire marital residence. It also directed that the sale be conducted by the sheriff or a special master chosen by Miracle Hills. The proceeds from the sale were to be brought before the court and applied towards satisfying the judgment. Although the decree referred to the foreclosure of Ali's undivided one-half interest, its sale provision covered the entire property. Ali challenged the decision, arguing that the lower court had improperly extended a judgment against one spouse to affect the ownership rights of the other.Homestead protection did not automatically prevent foreclosureOne of the central issues was whether Nebraska's homestead exemption protected the property from the creditor's action. Under state law, a qualifying homestead is generally protected from judgment liens and forced sales. The provisions are intended to safeguard a debtor and the family living in the home from losing their residence because of certain unpaid debts.However, the exemption is not automatic simply because a property is used as a family residence. Nebraska law requires the property owner to formally select it as a homestead through an application filed with the district court. The application must be filed before confirmation of the sale and provide specific information, including details about the judgment creditor, the circumstances supporting the exemption and the value of the claimed homestead. The required notice and procedural steps must also be followed.In this case, Ali had not filed an application satisfying those statutory requirements. Consequently, the homestead exemption could not be used to prevent the foreclosure proceedings. The court also clarified that the exemption was not an automatic restriction on the court's authority to enter a foreclosure decree. The legal protection depended on the required selection process, rather than residence alone.Supreme Court identified two errors in the sale decreeDespite rejecting Ali's homestead argument, the Nebraska Supreme Court found two significant errors in the district court's order. First, the judgment lien obtained by Miracle Hills attached only to Ali's undivided one-half interest in the jointly owned property. It did not extend to his wife's undivided one-half co-ownership interest because she was not responsible for the commercial lease debt.By ordering the sale of the entire residence, the lower court went beyond the interest covered by the creditor's lien. The distinction was important because a judgment against one spouse could not be used to subject the non-debtor spouse's ownership share to the same claim. Second, the decree failed to identify who would be responsible for conducting the sale. Leaving the decision to the sheriff or a special master selected by Miracle Hills gave one party discretion over a process involving opposing interests. The court determined that the decree needed to clearly identify the party authorised to carry out the sale. As a result, the Nebraska Supreme Court vacated the district court's decree and remanded the case for further proceedings.The decision does not eliminate Miracle Hills' judgment lien against Ali's one-half interest. However, the Supreme Court did not decide whether an equitable foreclosure action was proper in these circumstances. Any revised order must respect the limits of the creditor's lien and identify the party responsible for conducting the sale.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
